Davies reads that doctrine cybernetically, and the reading is colder than the usual moral complaint about greed. Handing a corporation the single objective maximize shareholder returns is an act of radical attenuation – it compresses every signal the machine might attend to, from worker safety to product quality to the long-term survival of its own suppliers, into one number, and then wires the whole control system to that number. In Beer's anatomy, it amputates System Five and solders a metric where identity used to be. A machine so configured does not need wicked executives to behave wickedly; it needs only to run. Davies pairs the doctrine with a second economic export, Goodhart's law – when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure – and notes the combination: modern institutions were instructed to govern themselves by targets, by a profession whose own law says targets rot. The rot is not hypothetical; it has a case file. When England's emergency departments were set a four-hour maximum wait, hospitals discovered patients could be held in ambulances outside the door, where the clock had not yet started, or admitted to a ward at hour three fifty-nine whether admission served them or not. The target was met; the thing the target stood for was not; and the information the measure once carried – how long sick people actually wait – was destroyed by the act of managing to it. A machine wired to a metric does not merely pursue the metric. It consumes it. Now, this is the point in the book where a listener should feel the ground tilt, because the argument is at its most satisfying here, and most-satisfying is exactly when this series applies the brakes. Ed Smith, reviewing the book in the New Statesman, pushed back on precisely this chapter: Davies, he argued, gives economics too much of the blame – the hollowing-out of responsibility has sources older and deeper than Friedman, and a discipline is a convenient defendant because it cannot take the stand. I think the objection lands about halfway. Davies does not claim economists invented the machine; he claims they wrote the objective function that the machine's most powerful instances now run – and for corporations since nineteen eighty, that claim seems to me simply true, and Smith does not really contest it. Where Smith wins is scope: the squirrels died, and the Post Office prosecuted, inside institutions where shareholder value explains nothing. The sink predates the doctrine. Friedman supplied one master objective; the tendency of large systems to shed responsibility needed no instruction. Keep both halves – the machine is old, its most aggressive current programming is recent – and you hold the book's argument at its honest strength, which is where an argument should be held before you decide how much of it to keep.

Chapter Seven: The Man Who Was Refused

Return, before closing, to Santiago, because the biography now reads differently than it did in chapter one. Beer was not a crank at the margins. He ran operations research for one of Britain's largest steel companies, commanded enormous consulting fees, wrote books that were reviewed and read. In the mid nineteen-seventies, at the height of his earning power, he gave most of it up – resigned the directorships, shed the possessions, and moved to a stone cottage in rural Wales with no telephone, where he wrote, painted, and taught for the rest of his life; whatever else can be said of him, he was not optimizing shareholder value. And across the nineteen seventies and eighties, his science died anyway – not refuted, Davies emphasizes, but defunded, unfashionable, orphaned between departments; too mathematical for the management schools, too managerial for the mathematicians, and, after the coup, politically radioactive by association. The discipline that asked how should an organization be wired so that it can perceive and correct itself lost the century to the discipline that asked how do rational agents maximize – and part of Davies's project is the claim that this was a wrong turn taken by Western thought as a whole, with the squirrels and the postmasters among its eventual invoices. It is a grand claim, and its grandness is worth noticing, because a book that began as a sharp essay about phone trees is now asserting that a forgotten Welshman's consultant had the correct theory of institutions and civilization declined to hear it. Ed Smith, in the same review, caught this too, from the other side: having introduced Beer, he complained, Davies does not actually give us much of him as a solution – the exhumation is loving, the reanimation thin. Whether that is a flaw in the book or an honest report on the state of the science is the question part three exists to answer. Because everything so far has been diagnosis, and diagnosis was the easy half. The machine decides; the machine is misaligned; the machine's own structure routes the evidence of its failures away from anyone who could act. The question a clinician asks next is the only one left. What is the treatment – and who, exactly, would administer it? Next time, Part Three: repairing the feedback. Thanks for listening.

item.title: The Unaccountability Machine, Part Three: Repairing the Feedback
item.description: The final part on Dan Davies's book: what repair would actually take, the critics given their full say, the synthesis with Rao and Jackall extended, and a verdict with a dose.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: The Industry That Chose the Other Road

Two parts of diagnosis have earned one part of treatment, and the treatment discussion should start with an industry that actually took it – one worked example, run to its end, and then held up against everything this series has described. This example is mine, assembled in Davies's terms rather than taken from his book, and it is commercial aviation. On the evening of December twenty-eighth, nineteen seventy-eight, a United Airlines DC-8 approached Portland, Oregon, with a hundred and eighty-one people aboard, and a landing-gear indicator light failed to come on. The captain, prudently, entered a holding pattern to troubleshoot. Then he kept holding. For the better part of an hour the aircraft circled a city full of runways while the captain worked the gear problem, and the flight engineer's remarks about the fuel gauges grew from observations into hints into something just short of a warning – and never crossed into the sentence that mattered, because one did not say that sentence to a captain. The engines flamed out from fuel exhaustion six miles short of the airport. Ten people died in a crash that had at no point involved anything being wrong with the airplane's ability to land. The cockpit voice recorder preserved the whole slow catastrophe: a subordinate who saw the error, and deference that attenuated the alarm to a whisper. Portland was not unique; a string of accidents in those years showed the same signature, a fatal fact known inside the cockpit and unable to travel four feet to the left. The industry faced a version of the Post Office's choice. It possessed a continuous stream of feedback about its own failures, and a hierarchy configured to attenuate that feedback into silence. What it built instead has become the standard story of institutional repair, and the details are the interesting part. Crew resource management retrained the cockpit so that challenging the captain became procedure rather than insubordination – a deliberate re-wiring of who may send information upward. Confidential reporting systems let any crew member file a safety report, in the American case to NASA, an agency outside the airline entirely, with limited immunity attached – so that the fear of blame, the force that scripts every helpline, was structurally disconnected from the act of reporting. Investigations were assigned to a board whose findings cannot be used to establish liability, on the explicit theory that an investigation which can punish will be lied to. And none of it is accountability in the political sense: no one demanded a named villain per crash. It is the opposite bet: that if you want the truth about a system's failures, you must make the truth safe to tell, and that punishing individuals for systemic errors does not produce fewer errors, it produces quieter ones. Commercial aviation is now so safe that its fatal-accident rate is measured per tens of millions of flights. The industry did not get there by finding better people. It got there by re-plumbing the feedback – which is to say, aviation is what it looks like when an institution reads Beer's diagnosis and actually fills the prescription.

Chapter Two: What the Book Itself Prescribes

So the repair is possible; an entire industry is the proof. What does Davies himself prescribe? Here honesty about the book requires a change of tone, because the answer is: less than the diagnosis deserves, and the critics noticed. The book's constructive argument runs at the level of principle. Sinks should be visible: an organization ought to know where it has delegated decisions to process, and treat each such delegation as a design choice someone owns, rather than sediment. Feedback links, once severed, should be rebuilt – the person affected by a policy needs some path to a person able to change it, and the two tests from part one, who holds the override and is anyone listening downstream, are the audit questions. Institutions need their System Four back: a funded, empowered function whose job is to perceive what the operational machine is structurally unable to see, including the machine's own victims. And the objective function is a choice: a corporation wired to a single metric is not a law of nature but a nineteen-seventies design decision that can, in principle, be revised. All of this follows from the diagnosis, and all of it is stated in the book more as direction than as blueprint. Tim Harford, whose Financial Times review was among the most sympathetic the book received, put the underlying principle in one sentence that is better than a paragraph of mine: without feedback, nothing ever gets better. But here the case against begins: a direction is not a mechanism, and a diagnosis that ends in principles is exactly the kind of output that the machines this book describes have proven magnificently capable of absorbing without changing.

Chapter Three: The Case Against, at Full Strength

This series steelmans before it criticizes, and it has spent two and a half episodes steelmanning; the critics now get their innings, stated as hard as the sources state them. The first count is the one just opened: the remedy is thin. Ed Smith, in the New Statesman, having praised the diagnosis as provocative and often brilliant, observed that Davies exhumes Stafford Beer with enormous care and then gives us surprisingly little of him as an actual solution – the rescue mission recovers the body, not the working science. On this count I think the defense is partial at best. One can argue, as I did last episode, that the thinness honestly reflects the state of a defunded discipline; but a book subtitled why big systems make terrible decisions raises the expectation that it knows what better ones would look like, and mostly it gestures. Aviation shows the prescription can be filled; it is not Davies who shows it. The second count is Smith's deeper objection, and it deserves slow statement because it is the best single criticism of the book I have found. Davies's whole framework, Smith argues, is built on the wrong noun. Accountability is an audit concept – it is about the traceability of decisions after the fact, and it is zero-sum: assigning more of it to me assigns less of it to you. What institutions have actually lost, Smith contends, is responsibility, which is something else entirely: the internalized, forward-looking sense of ownership that makes a professional fix a problem no rulebook assigned to them. And responsibility, unlike accountability, is not zero-sum – a whole ward, a whole cockpit, can hold it simultaneously without dividing it. The distinction bites, because you can imagine an organization that passes every one of Davies's audits – sinks mapped, overrides named, feedback channels built – in which no human being feels responsible for anything: a perfectly instrumented machine, fully accountable, morally vacant. The re-plumbed cockpit worked, on this reading, not mainly because the channels changed but because the culture that flowed through them did. The third count is the one conceded last episode and worth logging formally: the economics chapter over-claims. The sink predates Friedman, flourishes in ministries that have never had a shareholder, and would survive his doctrine's repeal. And a fourth count, mine: the book's charm is a risk factor. The accountability sink is such a satisfying concept – it explains one's last twenty customer-service calls in three words – that it invites the identity dose this series keeps warning about: the reader who sees sinks everywhere, files every institutional encounter under a diagnosis, and mistakes the filing for understanding. The Moral Mazes episode issued the same warning about Jackall, and the failure mode here is the same one wearing systems-theory clothes: taken as identity, the sink concept teaches that resistance is a category error – the machine decided, no one can be reached, why call the helpline at all – and a person who has fully internalized that lesson has done the machine's attenuation for it, free of charge. The book's own framework says to distrust any idea that reliably produces resignation in the people who hold it; applied to itself, that test is worth running. A framework this fluent should be handled like any potent diagnostic: indicated uses, known interactions, maximum dose.

Chapter Four: The Shelf, Rewired Once More

Episode two of this feed proposed a synthesis: Davies's sink as the industrialized successor of Rao's hand-built heads-I-win-tails-you-lose schemes, with Jackall's blame hydraulics as the missing middle chapter. Three episodes of slow walking let that synthesis carry more weight now, and one extension of it. Jackall's corporation conserved blame – it flowed downhill into a designated person. Davies's machine dissolves blame – it flows into process and vanishes. What the slow walk adds is where the conserved quantity went, and the answer is Beer's: what the sink actually destroys is not blame but information. Every severed feedback link is a channel down which the organization has chosen not to know something. The Post Office did not merely avoid blame for sixteen years; it purchased, at the price of scripting one helpline, the ability not to know what seven hundred prosecutions were built on. Blame was always the decoy. The real transaction in every sink is epistemic – and that is why the repair, wherever it has actually worked, has been epistemic too: aviation did not redistribute blame better, it made knowledge cheaper than denial. Which folds Rao's cynical layer back in with a colder eye. The sociopath layer, in this vocabulary, are not the people who escape blame; they are the people who position themselves where the unattenuated information still flows, and who hold override authority they are careful never to exercise on the record. And the extension explains, at last, why Rao's Powertalk belongs in this story. Episode two called it the unattenuated channel – the private language in which the powerful exchange the full-variety information the official channels compress away. The three-part version can now say what that arrangement is: it is a private algedonic wire, built by and for the people at the top, running alongside an official network they have allowed to go deaf. The organization does not lack the capacity to know; the capacity has been privatized. Beer wanted the alarm wire to serve the whole system. The sociopath layer builds one and keeps it. Find the accountability sink, this series said in episode two, and you have found the org chart. The three-part version is sharper: find what the organization has arranged not to know, and you have found what it is actually optimizing – the purpose of a system is what it refuses to hear.

Chapter Five: The Test Applied at Home

Before the verdict, one more application, constructed rather than drawn from the book, because a framework should be tested on ground the tester knows – and the ground this listener knows best is clinical research. Run Beer's anatomy over a randomized trial, and something unexpected appears: the apparatus of trial oversight is one of the few places where modern institutions have deliberately built the machinery this book says is missing. Consider what a data safety monitoring board actually is. A trial's investigators are, in the machine's terms, System One through Three: running operations, coordinating sites, controlling quality – and structurally incapable of judging their own trial's emerging harms, not because they are dishonest but because they are attenuated by their own hopes and blinded by design. So the institution wires in an external organ: an independent board that sees the unblinded data the investigators must not see, meets on its own schedule, answers to no one on the payroll, and holds the one authority that matters – the authority to stop the machine. That is a designed sink, in exactly Harford's sense. Responsibility for the stopping decision has been deliberately taken away from the people closest to the work, and everyone can point to the charter when asked who decided. But it is a sink with its feedback intact: the board exists precisely to receive the signal – accumulating harm – that the operational layers cannot be trusted to hear, and it is welded to an override. Serious adverse event reporting is the algedonic channel from last episode, a pain signal that regulation forbids anyone to attenuate on its way up. And the machinery goes one step further, in a detail worth savoring because it answers the corruption worry from part one: the stopping rules themselves are written in advance. A trial's statistical boundary for early stopping is chosen and documented before anyone knows which arm is winning – which means the single most consequential decision the system can face has been made by people who could not yet know whom it would favor. That is a System Five acting while it is still impartial, binding its future self against its future temptations; Ulysses at the mast, rewritten as a statistical analysis plan. The apparatus is imperfect, and every researcher can name trials where the wiring failed. But the design is Beer's design, discovered independently by a profession that had watched what happens without it, and it suggests a rule the book itself never quite states: the question is not whether to build sinks – complex work will always delegate decisions to structures – but whether each sink is built with its senses on, its alarm wire uncut, and its stop authority in hands that can be found. A field that can name where its own machinery is missing those three things has, in this book's terms, already begun the repair.

Chapter Six: Verdict, Dose, and a Question for Monday

The verdict, then, on the book this series has lived inside. The Unaccountability Machine is the rare popular book whose central concept enters the language because the language had a hole where it belonged, and its second half – the Beer exhumation – is more ambitious and more flawed than its famous first: a genuinely important intellectual rescue that stops short of teaching the rescued science to work. Read it whole, but read it as a diagnosis with a bibliography, not a diagnosis with a cure. The dose: one careful read for anyone who runs anything, from a research group to a health system; a re-read of the cybernetic chapters for anyone designing an organization from scratch, because the five-systems anatomy is the closest thing to a checklist the book contains. Three kinds of reader need it most: the person newly given authority over a process they did not build, who must decide which of its sinks are load-bearing; the person on the receiving end of a machine, who needs the vocabulary to see that the wall in front of them is architecture rather than malice; and the designer of anything – a trial, a dashboard, a reporting line – who is, whether the job title says so or not, choosing right now which information the future will be unable to hear. Pair it, against its own thinness of remedy, with the aviation-safety literature, where the prescription has case law; and pair it against its own charm with Smith's correction, that a system can be perfectly accountable and no one in it responsible – carry both nouns, and ask which one an institution is actually short of, because the treatments differ: an accountability deficit is fixed with wiring, and a responsibility deficit is fixed, if it can be fixed at all, with culture, hiring, and time. And the question to carry into Monday, this series' standing custom, assembled from all three parts. When you next hit the wall – the policy that is the policy, the denial no one signed – do not begin with who is to blame, because part one showed that door is welded. Ask instead: what has this organization arranged not to know, and what would it cost anyone here to find out? If the answer is that knowing is expensive and not-knowing is free, you are not looking at a mistake. You are looking at the machine, running as built – and now you know the two points where machines like it have actually been rebuilt: make the truth safe to tell, and give someone, someone findable, the authority to act on it. Next time, the book this whole shelf descends from, the one Rao read chapter by chapter before writing a word of the Gervais Principle: William Whyte's The Organization Man. Thanks for listening.

item.title: The Unaccountability Companion: Dan Davies, from Lying for Money to the Accountability Sink
item.description: An analysis of Dan Davies's body of work — Lying for Money, The Unaccountability Machine, and the Back of Mind newsletter — synthesized with Rao's Gervais Principle: sinks as industrialized HIWTYL, the clueless middle as the sink's human interface, and Powertalk as the unattenuated channel.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter 1: Who Dan Davies is

Dan Davies's The Unaccountability Machine is the natural third leg of the stool this series has been building, alongside Rao and Jackall. So this episode is a tour of Davies's whole body of work, ending in a synthesis with the Gervais Principle. First, who is he — and a disambiguation, since there are two British writers named Dan Davies, and the other one wrote a biography of Jimmy Savile. Our Davies is a Welsh former Bank of England regulatory economist turned investment-bank analyst, and before he was an author he was one of the great bloggers of the early internet, writing as D-squared Digest through the two thousands. That blog matters for understanding everything after, because it established his method and his most quoted idea: what he called the one-minute MBA, whose first and most famous lesson was that good ideas do not need lots of lies told about them in order to gain public acceptance — written about the case for the Iraq war, and holding up remarkably well since. His signature register was set there too: whimsical, contrarian, allergic to moralizing, and convinced that the most interesting truths about institutions live in their plumbing rather than their pronouncements. He now writes a Substack called Back of Mind, subtitled a newsletter of quiet contrarianism, slow analysis and ambient ideas, which is the living laboratory where his books get thought out in public. The corpus, then: Lying for Money in twenty eighteen, a theory of fraud. The Unaccountability Machine in twenty twenty-four, a theory of organizational decision-making built on the cybernetics of Stafford Beer. A book on the Brompton folding bicycle company, about manufacturing and process knowledge. And the newsletter stitching it together. The through-line, which I'll try to convince you of by the end: Davies has spent twenty-five years writing one long book about the same subject — how trust, information, and blame move through systems that have grown too big for anyone to hold in their head.

Chapter 2: Lying for Money — fraud as an information problem

Start with the fraud book, because it contains the seed of everything. Lying for Money is nominally a tour of great financial frauds — pyramid schemes, counterfeits, cartels, control frauds — organized into a working taxonomy. But its real subject is trust, treated as an economic quantity. Davies's central move is to point out that checking things is expensive. A modern economy works because we mostly don't verify — we trust certificates, audits, invoices, titles, and each other — and this non-checking is not laziness but the whole source of the productivity. Fraud, in his definition, is an attack on that trust infrastructure: the fraudster finds a place where society has decided checking isn't worth the cost, and moves in. Which yields the book's most famous and most clinical conclusion: the optimal level of fraud is not zero. A society with zero fraud would be a society that verified everything, and it would be poor, slow, and miserable — a low-trust world. Fraud is, quite literally, the tax we pay on the efficiency of trusting. He illustrates with what he calls the Canadian paradox: why does laid-back, high-trust Canada have such a lively history of securities fraud, while low-trust societies have less? Because you can only be defrauded where trust exists. Fraud is a disease of advanced trust economies the way certain infections are diseases of hospitals. Notice the shape of this argument, because it recurs: take a phenomenon everyone treats as a moral failing of individuals, and redescribe it as a structural property of information flows — with an equilibrium level, trade-offs, and no satisfying villain. And notice something else, relevant to our synthesis: the fraudster in Lying for Money is recognizably Rao's sociopath in the wild. He is precisely the person who has noticed which parts of the collective performance are load-bearing and unguarded. Davies just declines to be scandalized about it.

Chapter 3: The Unaccountability Machine — the sink

Now the main event. The Unaccountability Machine, from twenty twenty-four, opens with an image that has already entered the language: the accountability sink. Davies's canonical illustration is an airline story from the nineteen nineties, in which hundreds of squirrels arriving as cargo without proper paperwork were destroyed — fed into a shredder — by ground staff following the applicable procedure, to public horror. The question the book hangs on that horror: who, exactly, decided to do that? The staff followed policy. The policy authors never met a squirrel. The managers enforced compliance with a rulebook written for good reasons. Everyone did their job, the outcome was monstrous, and there is genuinely no one to blame. That is an accountability sink: a structure in which decision-making has been delegated to a process, and the crucial link — the feedback link between the person affected by a decision and anyone capable of changing it — has been severed. You have met the sink. It is the phone tree that disconnects you, the insurance denial that no human at the company can override, the hospital discharge decided by an algorithm no one in the building can explain. Davies's sharpest observation is that sinks are not accidents and not exactly evil: they are how large organizations metabolize more complexity than any individual can process. Delegating decisions to a rulebook is what lets a system scale. But he also states what he calls the principle of diminishing accountability: unless conscious steps are taken to prevent it, any organization in a modern society will restructure itself to reduce the personal responsibility attributable to its actions — and this tendency continues until crisis. Sinks accumulate, in other words, because they are individually rational and collectively corrosive. The diagnostic test he offers is beautifully simple. Ask of any bad outcome: was there anyone with the authority to override the policy? If yes, you have accountability. If the answer is the policy is the policy, you are standing in the sink.

Chapter 4: Stafford Beer and the cybernetic spine

What elevates the book beyond a catalogue of bureaucratic horror is its second half, which is a rescue mission for a nearly forgotten intellectual tradition: the management cybernetics of Stafford Beer, the flamboyant British consultant best known for building Project Cybersyn, a real-time economic control room for Allende's Chile that died with the nineteen seventy-three coup. Davies extracts three ideas from Beer that you should file permanently. First, POSIWID: the purpose of a system is what it does. Not what its mission statement says, not what its leaders intend — if a system reliably produces an outcome, treat that outcome as its purpose and analyze accordingly. A hospital billing department that reliably generates surprise bills is, functionally, a surprise-bill-generating system, whatever its values slide says. It's the most clarifying four-letter acronym in organizational thought. Second, Ashby's law of requisite variety: a controller must have at least as much variety — as many possible states — as the thing it's controlling. When it doesn't, it must attenuate: compress reality into categories, dashboards, and forms. Every organization is therefore an engine for throwing away information, and the design question is only ever which information gets discarded. The squirrels died in an attenuation: whatever was individual about that situation had been compressed to a paperwork category with one procedure attached. Third, and most striking, Beer's claim — which Davies updates for the AI age — that organizations should be understood as artificial intelligences: genuinely decision-making entities whose goals are distinct from the intentions of any member, running on people the way software runs on chips. We spent the twenty-tens fretting about misaligned AI, Davies observes, while already living inside misaligned AIs called corporations and ministries. The book's villain, incidentally, is the economics that blessed all this — particularly the Friedman-era doctrine that a firm's only responsibility is shareholder value, which Davies reads as the ideological license to install one master sink at the top of every corporation.

Chapter 5: The blog and the Brompton — process knowledge

Before synthesizing, two quicker stops that round out the picture. The Brompton book — about the London folding-bicycle manufacturer — sounds like a departure and isn't. It's a study in process knowledge: the tacit, accumulated, embodied know-how that lives in a workshop's hands and habits and can't be written down, offshored, or acquired in a merger. It is, in cybernetic terms, a book about the information that must not be attenuated — the variety a viable system has to keep in-house. If The Unaccountability Machine is about what organizations destroy by compressing information, The Brompton is the affirmative case: what it looks like when an organization protects its unattenuated knowledge, even at the cost of staying small and slightly eccentric. James C. Scott's metis — the local knowledge that legibility schemes destroy — is the same idea wearing different clothes, which tells you Davies and Rao are, in places, mining the same vein. Then there's Back of Mind, the Substack, which I'd genuinely recommend as one of the best ongoing feeds of institutional thinking anywhere. It's where the books breathe: essays applying the toolkit to whatever's in the news — regulatory disasters, opinion polling, judicial review, why certification regimes fail when everyone obeys rules to the letter with no margin, an idea he calls stacked tolerances that deserves wider currency. Recent posts have even wandered directly onto Rao's turf, including one titled middle management is what the other guy does. The register throughout is the opposite of the systems-collapse doomer genre: cheerful, unscandalized, fixated on mechanism. Davies writes about institutional dysfunction the way a good clinician writes about disease — as a professional who finds pathology interesting and believes in treatment.

Chapter 6: The synthesis — Rao's people, Davies's plumbing

Now the payoff — laying Davies over the Gervais Principle, because the overlap you sensed is real, and the disagreement is even more interesting. Both writers are staring at the same phenomenon: organizations systematically route blame away from power. But they tell opposite stories about the mechanism. Rao's account is agent-centric: sociopaths deliberately construct heads-I-win-tails-you-lose structures, and the clueless middle exists to absorb liability. Blame, for Rao, flows downhill into a person. Davies's account is structure-centric: blame flows into a process, and vanishes. Nobody absorbs it, because the sink's whole function is that there is no body. Jackall's managers said blame flows down; Davies says the mature machine improves on that — blame flows nowhere. Here's my proposed synthesis, and I think it's stronger than either book alone. The accountability sink is the industrialized, scaled-up successor of Rao's HIWTYL scheme. A heads-I-win-tails-you-lose arrangement is artisanal — it must be hand-built for each situation, and it still needs a designated loser, which is inefficient and leaves evidence. A sink automates it: build the deniability into procedure once, and it runs forever, protecting everyone above it, with no individual scapegoat required and therefore no one with a grievance. And this suggests where the layers of Rao's pyramid actually stand relative to the sink. The sociopath layer are the sink's architects — the people who commission rulebooks, choose the metrics, decide which variety gets attenuated, and, crucially, retain for themselves the override authority that Davies says defines real accountability. The clueless middle is the sink's human interface — the sincere enforcers who say the policy is the policy and mean it, converting reality into the categories the system can digest. Manufacturing legibility, as we said last time; operating the attenuator, as Beer would say. And Powertalk? Powertalk is the unattenuated channel. It's how the architects exchange the full-variety information — who's really exposed, what the numbers really mean — that the official channels were designed to compress away. The formal org chart runs on attenuated information; the sociopath network runs on the raw feed. That, I'd argue, is the deepest single insight the two frameworks produce together: power in an organization is exactly the question of who gets the unattenuated information, and who possesses override authority over the sinks. Find those two things and you've found the real org chart.

Chapter 7: Verdict — which theory to reach for when

So how should you hold these two bodies of work together? They correct each other's characteristic error, almost perfectly. Rao's failure mode is paranoia: everything is somebody's scheme, every structure hides an author, and the reader is trained to hunt sociopaths — which over-attributes agency, and in real institutions leads you to accuse people of designing dysfunctions that nobody designed. Davies's failure mode is the opposite — call it exoneration: the system did it, everyone followed procedure, responsibility dissolves into cybernetics, and the reader half-forgets that sinks have beneficiaries, that somewhere there were architects who chose this attenuation over that one, and that the principle of diminishing accountability advances because specific people, with names, profit from each increment. Even one of the strongest critiques of Davies's book lands here: it's diagnostically brilliant and thin on remedy. The combined lens avoids both errors. When something goes wrong in your institution, run Davies first: map the sink, find where the feedback link was cut, ask who holds override authority — because most dysfunction really is structural, and hunting for villains in a structural failure wastes your outrage and your credibility. But then run Rao second: ask who benefits from this sink's existence, who built it, who is exempt from it — because sinks are not weather; they are architecture, and architecture has clients. In Beer's terms: the purpose of a system is what it does, and what it reliably does for the people at the top is worth particular attention. As for the reading order, if this episode sends you to the shelf: The Unaccountability Machine first — it's the most complete and the most relevant to this decade, AI included. Lying for Money second, because it's the most purely enjoyable and the trust framework generalizes everywhere, from finance to peer review. Then subscribe to Back of Mind and let the toolkit compound weekly. Davies is, I think, the rare writer who took everything true in the cynical tradition we've been touring — Rao's sharpness, Jackall's blame hydraulics — and rebuilt it as engineering rather than demonology. Which makes him not just an overlap with the Gervais Principle, but arguably its adult supervision. Thanks for listening.

item.title: Episode One: Moral Mazes, or the Bureaucratic Ethic
item.description: Robert Jackall went into two American corporations the way an anthropologist goes up a river, and came back with the rules managers actually live by. The founding text of the cynical core.
item.content:encoded:
Chapter One: Why We Start Here

Welcome back to the Annotated Shelf. Last time was a smoke test; this time the machine gets a real book, and I want to start with the one that anchors the whole series. Published in nineteen eighty-eight, Robert Jackall's Moral Mazes is the finest piece of fieldwork ever conducted on the American corporate manager, and I mean fieldwork in the anthropologist's sense, as if Jackall had gone up the Sepik River with a notebook, except the river was a chemical company in New Jersey and the tribe wore suits. Everything else on this shelf, from Venkatesh Rao's sociopath-clueless-loser pyramid to Dan Davies's accountability sinks, is in some way a footnote, a formalization, or a rediscovery of what Jackall found. Rao says so openly; Davies might as well. If you read one book from the cynical core of this series, it should be this one. One promise before we start. This is the bleakest book on the shelf, and I am going to present its findings at full strength, because diluted Jackall is useless. But hold on to the dosage rule this series lives by: cynical frameworks are medicine at diagnostic doses and poison at identity doses, and the final chapter will be about how to swallow this one safely. So let's find out what he actually saw.

Chapter Two: The Sociologist Who Got Inside

Jackall was a sociology professor at Williams College, and the origin story matters. In the early nineteen-eighties he set out to study how corporate managers think about ethics, and dozens of companies turned him down flat, which is itself a data point. The access he finally won, after months of courtship, was to a large chemical products conglomerate and a big textile firm, plus a public relations agency, all disguised under pseudonyms. He then did something almost nobody does: he hung around for years. Not surveys, not a week of interviews. He sat in on meetings, ate in the cafeterias, followed reorganizations as they happened, and interviewed managers at every level, again and again, until they stopped performing for him. The book's subtitle is The World of Corporate Managers, and the word world is doing real work. Jackall's claim is that the corporation is not a neutral instrument that people bring their morals into. It is a world, with its own gods, its own rituals, and its own ethic, and it remakes the people inside it. One structural detail from his account is worth fixing in your mind before we go further, because everything else depends on it: in these companies, credentials got you in the door, but after that, advancement past a certain grade had almost nothing to do with measured competence, which was simply assumed, the way an officer corps assumes everyone can ride. What was actually being judged, continuously and unforgivingly, was style: self-control, appearance, the ability to absorb a superior's anxiety without transmitting any of your own, and above all the perception by powerful seniors that you were, in the standard phrase, someone we can be comfortable with. Managers called the whole arrangement a probation that never ends. His name for the ethic it produces is the bureaucratic ethic, and his one-line summary of it is the most quoted sentence in the book, from a manager he interviewed: what is right in the corporation is what the guy above you wants from you. Under fifteen words, and it earns its fame.

Chapter Three: Morality as a Function of Reporting Lines

Slow that sentence down, because it is easy to hear it as a complaint and it is actually a description of a mechanism. Jackall's managers were not villains. Most of them were, by their own lights, decent family men, and off the clock they held perfectly ordinary moral views. The finding is that those views were checked at the door, not out of cowardice exactly, but because the organization gave them no purchase. Here is a worked example, and I should flag that the scenario is constructed, though it is assembled from the patterns Jackall documents. A plant manager learns that fixing a safety problem will cost two million dollars and blow this year's numbers. His boss has made it clear, without ever saying anything actionable, that the numbers are the priority. If the manager escalates in writing, he has created a document, and creating documents about problems is understood as an aggressive act, because it pins responsibility to a name. If he pays for the fix, he misses his targets, and missed targets are the one sin with a fixed penalty. If he does nothing and the problem surfaces in four years, the odds are excellent that he will have been promoted twice and be somewhere else entirely. Every incentive points one way. Jackall's point is that you do not need bad people to get this outcome. You need only ordinary people, a steep hierarchy, short time horizons, and the rule that your boss is your primary moral audience. The manager who follows his private conscience is not punished for being ethical. He is punished for being unpredictable, which in this world is worse.

Chapter Four: The Hydraulics of Blame

The second great insight is what I call, and will keep calling all series, blame hydraulics. In Jackall's corporations, details are pushed down and credit is pulled up. A senior executive states an objective at a level of grand vagueness, make the environmental problem go away, and each layer below translates it into something more specific, so that by the time anything concrete and possibly indictable is happening, it is happening far from the person who willed it. Meanwhile credit flows the opposite direction, up through the same pipework, toward whoever is positioned at the top when results arrive. Two corollaries follow, and Jackall names both. First, milking. A manager who knows he will rotate roles in eighteen months has every reason to strip his current plant, defer maintenance, squeeze the working capital, and post beautiful numbers whose costs land on his successor. Jackall's managers had a word for inheriting such a situation: you had been left holding the bag. Second, outrunning your mistakes. Because performance is judged on short cycles and consequences mature on long ones, the career skill that matters most is not avoiding errors but being somewhere else when they detonate. Notice what this does to the very idea of a track record. It converts it from a history of outcomes into a history of exits. And notice, listeners who know their Davies, that an accountability sink, a structure no individual can be blamed for, is just blame hydraulics poured into concrete and given a compliance department. Jackall watched the fluid version, wet and moving, forty years earlier.

Chapter Five: Weather, Not Justice

There is a third finding, less quoted and, I would argue, more important than either of the first two. Jackall's managers did not experience their careers as the outcome of merit, and, crucially, not as the outcome of injustice either. They experienced them as weather. The word that comes up again and again in his interviews is luck, and the structural fact underneath the word is the reorganization. Every few years the corporation convulses. A new CEO arrives with a mandate, boxes on the chart are merged and split, and whole networks of patronage are beheaded overnight. Your fate in the shake-up depends not on your record but on your sponsor's fate, because in Jackall's world you rise as part of a patron's entourage, and when the patron falls, or merely loses a turf war three levels above your sight line, you fall with him, guilty of nothing except affiliation. Here is the constructed example. Two plant managers have identical numbers. One reports up through an executive who backed the winning side of a succession fight; the other's patron backed the loser. Eighteen months later the first is a division president and the second is managing, as Jackall's informants would put it, a warehouse in Odessa. Everyone around them knows the difference was nothing either man did. Now ask what a rational person does once he has internalized that fates are distributed like rainfall. He stops investing in outcomes, which the weather can wash away, and starts investing in the two things the weather cannot touch: his network of protectors and his reputation for being safe. Which is exactly the behavior the earlier chapters described, arrived at by a second, independent road. The maze does not need to teach cynicism by punishment. Ordinary probability theory, honestly applied to a patronage system, teaches it for free.

Chapter Six: The Management of Talk

And then there is language, which deserves its own chapter because Jackall gives it one of the sharpest treatments in the literature. In the maze, talk is never merely description; it is always positioning, and the system runs on a dialect built for deniability. Instructions flow downward in a form soft enough to disown. A superior never says, dump the waste at night. He says, this environmental thing is becoming a real problem for us, and trails off, and the subordinate's career depends on his skill at hearing the unsaid, doing the necessary, and never, ever, making the instruction explicit by asking for clarification in writing. Jackall calls the required talent gut feel, but notice that it is really a literacy, fluency in a language whose whole grammar exists so that meaning happened but no sentence did. The same dialect runs upward as euphemism. No one is fired; headcount is rationalized. No one lies to a regulator; the company advocates its position. And Jackall spends his final chapters on the purest speakers of the dialect, the public relations men, whose job he describes with some awe as the manufacture of plausible official realities, and who are candid with him in a way the line managers rarely manage, perhaps because a professional illusionist has no illusions left about himself. I will make one connection forward. When we get to Graeber's Bullshit Jobs, remember this chapter, because half of what Graeber's miserable informants describe, the box-ticking, the reports nobody reads, the meetings about meetings, is the maze's dialect made into full-time employment. The talk stopped being how the work is discussed and became the work.

Chapter Seven: The Shelf It Stands On

Where does the book itself stand? Squarely on Max Weber, and Jackall is explicit about it. Weber gave us the Protestant ethic, the idea that salvation anxiety got secularized into disciplined work, and also the theory of bureaucracy as rationalization. Jackall's move is to weld the two together and report that bureaucracy won: the Protestant ethic, where your work testified to your character before God, has been replaced by the bureaucratic ethic, where your work testifies to your alignment before your patron. Three companions earn their place beside it. Erving Goffman's Presentation of Self in Everyday Life, coming later in this series, supplies the micro-mechanics: Jackall tells you that self-presentation outweighs substance in the managerial world, and Goffman explains exactly how a self gets staged, teamed, and maintained. C. Wright Mills, in White Collar and in his essay on vocabularies of motive, supplies the language machinery, how organizations furnish their members with respectable reasons that are available for use, which is precisely what Jackall's managers reach for when they explain a layoff as a rationalization or a firing as a fit problem. And Rao's Gervais Principle, where this series began, is best read as Moral Mazes rewritten as comedy, with the office as sitcom rather than ethnography. Rao's sociopath layer, the people who see the game clearly and play it without illusion, are Jackall's most successful informants, the ones who told him the truth with a certain relish.

Chapter Eight: The Case Against

Now the case against, stated as hard as I can make it. First, sampling. Jackall studied two large, old-line, hierarchical industrial firms in the early eighties, companies already sliding toward decline, plus a PR agency chosen precisely because image-making is its product. That is a sample built to confirm the thesis. A fast-growing firm where the product either works or does not, or a partnership where the partners eat their own cooking, might have given him a different tribe. Second, vintage. The corporation of nineteen eighty-two, with its lifetime employment and its twenty-two grades of vice president, is not today's employer, and you could argue that markets for talent, equity compensation, and the sheer legibility of individual output in some modern industries have loosened the patronage system he describes. I only half believe that argument, since the same dynamics keep getting rediscovered by each generation, which suggests Jackall found something structural rather than something eighties. But the objection is fair and the burden is on the book's fans. Third, and most serious, the totalizing gloom. In Jackall's world no one ever successfully blows a whistle, holds a line, or builds a pocket of integrity that survives. Read at full identity dose, the book teaches learned helplessness: everything is politics, so why try. That conclusion outruns his evidence. His evidence shows that virtue is expensive and unrewarded in a certain organizational design, not that it is impossible, and later work on high-reliability organizations, and for that matter Ostrom's commons governance waiting at the end of this series, shows institutional designs where the incentives run otherwise.

Chapter Nine: The Series So Far, Rewired

Let me wire this into the series' running frames. Rao's pyramid answers a question Jackall leaves open: if the maze is this bleak, why does anyone stay? Rao's answer is that the layers stay for different currencies, the losers for security, the clueless for belonging, the sociopaths for power, which explains the maze's stability better than Jackall's own picture of universal anxiety. Davies answers a different open question: what happens when blame hydraulics get automated? The Unaccountability Machine's answer is that the fluid gets piped into formal structure, the accountability sink, at which point you no longer need the smoke-filled room or the patron's raised eyebrow, because the org chart itself performs the deniability. And Jackall gives the series something neither of the others has: moral weight. Rao is playing it for laughs and Davies for policy, but Jackall sat across from men who, in the safety of anonymity, told him plainly that they had surrendered their own judgment, and who seemed relieved that someone had finally asked. The maze is not just inefficient. It costs its inhabitants something, and they know it. That, incidentally, is why I resist the reading of Jackall as a cynic. A cynic would have found the surrenders funny, or at least deserved. Jackall reports them the way a doctor reports symptoms, and the anger under the flat prose is the anger of someone who believes moral agency is real and watched a machine designed, by nobody in particular, to buy it up cheap.

Chapter Ten: Verdict

My verdict. Moral Mazes is essential, and it is essential at diagnostic dose, one careful read, notes in the margins, and then back on the shelf. Taken as identity, as a total theory of working life, it will corrode you, because you will start reading every colleague's kindness as positioning, and the book's own evidence does not support that much cynicism. A diagnostic dose, to be concrete, means using it the way a doctor uses a pathology text, to recognize a condition when you meet it, not to conclude that every body is diseased. Who should read it: anyone in the first decade of a corporate career, before the water becomes invisible; anyone who designs incentive systems and still believes a values statement is an incentive; and anyone who has been left holding the bag and wants to know it has a name. The durable diagnostic to carry into Monday is this. When a decision lands on your desk, ask: who will be standing here when the consequences of this decision mature, and is anything in this room designed to make that person's interests present today? If the answer is no one and nothing, you are not making a decision. You are inside a maze, and the maze is making it. And the constructive corollary, since this series promises antidotes as well as diagnoses: whenever you do hold power over an incentive system, the single highest-leverage repair Jackall implies is to lengthen the feedback loop's reach, to make sure some consequences can still find their author after the author has moved. Everything else in the maze follows from the fact that, mostly, they cannot. Next time, Parkinson's Law, which is a much funnier book about the same machinery, and funnier on purpose. Thanks for listening.
